Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette:
For as long as Robert could remember, the cold was never just cold. He was six years old, sitting on the basement floor of the house in Cleveland, when his father had dragged him down the stairs by one arm and left him there without a coat. The concrete was freezing through his pajamas, and he had sat shivering for hours, listening to the furnace rumble above him, his own small heartbeat loud in his ears. That was the night he learned that the people who were supposed to protect him could be the ones who locked him in the dark. The memory came back now without warning—a sudden, unbidden image of the basement steps, the smell of coal dust, the cold seeping into his bones—and it would arrive in the middle of a workday, while he was reviewing code, and he would feel the temperature drop on his skin as if someone had opened a window onto a winter night.

Robert was sixty-six now, a software engineer who had spent forty years writing systems that ran on logic, on predictability. He lived in a quiet suburb with his wife, Ellen, and he had built a life that looked orderly from the outside. But the old vigilance had never left him. He had come to believe that danger was always waiting, that you could not afford to let your guard down for a single moment. When his heart began to pound—sometimes for no reason he could name—his body reacted before his mind had time to catch up, and he would find himself scanning the room for exits, for anything that could be used as a weapon. He noticed potential weapons everywhere now: a letter opener on a desk, a heavy book on a shelf, the sharp edge of a kitchen knife. His body was always a step ahead, and that only confirmed what he already knew—that he could not trust the world to be safe.

This constant vigilance had shaped the way he moved through his days. He avoided physical contact with others, flinching when a colleague clapped him on the shoulder, reacting with alarm when Ellen touched him unexpectedly from behind. He had stopped seeing old friends, the people he had socialized with before the memories started surfacing more frequently. It was easier to stay home, to keep his body to himself. But the isolation deepened his sense of being separate, of being permanently an outsider now. He watched couples walk down the street and felt that they belonged to a world he could no longer enter. People can't be trusted, he told himself, and the thought made him pull back further. The more he avoided, the more convinced he became that he was right to do so—that the distance between him and others was necessary, that it was the only way to stay safe.

The cold sensation on his skin would trigger the old memories, and the memories would trigger the vigilance, and the vigilance would make him notice the letter opener on the desk, and the noticing would make his heart race, and the racing heart would bring the memory back again. It was a loop that tightened over weeks and months, and Robert had learned to live inside it. He had stopped going to the grocery store. He had stopped answering the phone. Ellen had started doing the shopping alone, and she had stopped asking him to come along. That was the consequence he noticed most—the quiet way she had stopped hoping he would change.

What finally brought Robert to a therapist's office was not a crisis, but a quiet Tuesday afternoon. He had been sitting at his desk, staring at a line of code, when he felt the cold on his forearm and the memory rose up and he could not breathe for a moment. He realized, with a clarity that surprised him, that he had been waiting his whole life for something to change, and nothing had. He was afraid that this was all there would be—the basement, the cold, the vigilance, the loneliness—and he was also afraid that even talking about it would make it worse. But he came anyway, because he could not think of what else to do.
